text:
Arrigo was watching her: she had set her feet on the same footrest against which he himself pressed as he arched back to row; her short skirt had slipped up a little, and he could see her slender ankles emerging from her low-cut shoes, then rising with equal symmetry, like perfect spindles, and disappearing among the lace of her little skirt into the beginnings of darkness. She wore ash-colored silk stockings, openworked and gleaming. With the tips of her restless little feet, every now and then in play, she touched his. And they laughed, they both laughed, without speaking to each other.

In that peace, in the slowness of the rowing, in the rocking of the moving boat, they understood that the sweetest thing was to look at each other and be silent.

He observed her. In the sun, in the great blaze, her flesh took on a golden transparency, like the calyxes of tea roses; the down on her skin glistened minutely, and its shadows seemed darker. He examined her, and realized, perhaps for the first time, that she did not have a pure mouth, not the mouth of her twenty years, limpid and almost light like herself, but a sensual mouth, warm, too red, too alive, the mouth of a woman already much kissed, already versed in all the lusts that love teaches. And slackening in his stroke, his body leaning backward and his eyes half closed, he stretched beneath the kiss of that impure mouth with a long sensual shudder.

In the heat of the day, amid the glare of the dazzling sun, she too let her eyelids fall halfway over eyes somewhat intoxicated by the light; a sense of blissful weariness spread across her face, through her whole body, flooding her with repose as after exertion. And in her he no longer saw the girl who had skipped among the flowers in the garden, throwing pebbles into the fountains, but another, who bore on her lips the smile of the fallen woman, and seemed almost to be falling asleep after suffering a violent pleasure; another, whom he pictured lying in a bed of love, naked, her languid arms along her sides, abandoned in the sweet repose of the pleasure endured, naked and weary in a bed of love, her head turned to one side amid her half-loosened hair, her mouth moist, her eyes faded, dark as violets...

He rowed slowly, slowly, in the infinite light. One bank receded, the other was still far away; everything seemed to be yielding to sleep, to feel itself oppressed by the splendor, in that sunny afternoon. They passed near a fisherman, whose boat lay still and whose line was in the water. Slowly, without making a sound, they glided on.

He observed her: she held the two tiller cords, one in each hand; but both hands rested in her lap, half open, almost asleep, so that at the slightest tug of the rudder they might perhaps have let the two ropes slip away. The sun gilded those hands; they looked somewhat dark against the whiteness of her skirt. They too, like her mouth, revealed no purity. They were made for every sin, they were destined to inflict tormenting caresses, and in their innocent shape they bore some sign that betrayed their aptitude for vice. And across his hot face, across his somewhat parched mouth, over his whole body wearied by long desire, he felt the caress of those lascivious hands pass, a caress that enervated and twisted him, lavishing upon him a voluptuousness full of death, from the roots of his hair to his last veins. Then he let go of the oars, bent forward, and kissed her.

“What are you doing?...” she said as though awakening, astonished.

“I love you,” he replied, encircling her with his arms and looking into her sun-filled eyes, his whole body reaching and bending over her, his mouth immersed in her living breath. To shake herself free of that torpor, she stretched languidly beneath him as he weighed a little upon her, and, raising her arms, with a movement full of love she clasped them around his neck, throwing her head backward, closing her eyes, blissful.

Over the water, over all the water, the beating of their enamored souls seemed to race in a tremor of light.

“Kiss me...” she uttered, as though she wished to translate into words for him that fullness of joy which intoxicated her senses. “Kiss me once more, as you did before... like this... like this...”

He kissed her again upon her moist mouth, greedily, as one sucks a honeycomb. And she ran her fingers through his hair, uncovering his temples and forehead, slowly combing his hair with a lingering caress.

“I feel happy...” she repeated, her young throat swelling with her breath. “I should like to say so many inexpressible things... I should almost like to sing, yes, to sing for joy!...”

And she turned her eyes all around, over that infinite blaze, and it seemed to her that she embraced within herself all the splendor she saw.

He stared deeply at her, with a steadfast power in his eyes:

“You are mine, or what do you think?” he asked breathlessly, almost angrily. And he clasped her so tightly in his rough arms that she seemed to feel pain from it.

“Why do you ask me that? Why are you acting like this?...” she said, with a shadow of fear.

“Nothing, it is nothing... pay no attention to what I say. Laugh, Loretta, laugh again!”

And he rose and began rowing once more. Over his face had again descended that expression of violence and torment which often distorted it; his extraordinarily agile body bent and straightened, impetuous in the effort of pulling hard at the oars; the slender little boat sped along; the lashed water leapt in swift rainbows.

“What is the matter with you? Why are you tiring yourself like this?”

He did not answer; indeed, he rowed harder.

“Let me try,” she said. “I want to row too.”

And she made as if to rise.

“Do not move, do not move, or you will fall.”

“I want to row too; let me try.”

“Yes, wait.” And, panting, he abandoned the oars.

“How strong you are! We were going so fast just now!”

He smiled at her as he wiped away the sweat that ran down his forehead.

“So you want to row?”

“Yes.”

“Very well, let us try: I shall sit on the other bench and you will come here.”

He changed places, put another pair of oars into the water, and held out a hand to support her as she crossed over. When she was seated, he kissed her again on the nape and the temple, encircled her, and held her captive. Laughing, she pressed her cheek against his bare neck; then she said:

“Why did you ask me that question, Rigo?”

“I wanted to know whether you love me, whether you truly love me...” he replied with a lover’s timidity.

“Do you not know it, then?”

He did not answer; he taught her how to hold the oars and guided her arm through the stroke.

“It is easy!” the girl replied. “You see that I know how to row too?”
